title: "Browser apps"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette

Two apps put a graphical interface on the packages. The
[R app](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/theoryforge/apps/r/) runs this package
through [webR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/), a build of R for the
browser, and the
[Python app](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/theoryforge/apps/py/) runs the
Python package through [Pyodide](https://pyodide.org/). Each app loads the
package's own source into the browser and runs it there, so its results are
those of the package, and nothing about a theory is sent to a server. The first
visit downloads the language engine, which takes a while, and the browser keeps
it for later visits.

## What the apps do

A theory comes from the list of examples, from a YAML or JSON file uploaded from
your computer or from the editor. A card beside it shows whether the package
finds it valid, its rigour score and gate, the number of its constructs,
propositions and predictions, and its content hash. The score and the hash
follow a moment after the rest, and a theory with more than 300 constructs,
propositions and predictions is scored and hashed only when you ask, since
either can take a long time on a theory that size. You choose an operation, set
its parameters and run it, and the result appears with a note on what it shows.
Figures can be saved as SVG or PNG, text and JSON results as files, and the
preregistration and the dossier are shown as formatted pages with their Markdown
a click away.

The operations are grouped by purpose. Assess holds the rigour checklist, the
full validation, the claim-form rubric, post-data severity and the redundancy
screen. Derive holds the implied conditional independencies, what the causal
graph entails, the equivalent models and the lavaan syntax. Compare sets the
theory against a rival, which is either an alternative that states its own
propositions or a theory you upload, and appraises an amendment against a prior
version, by default the version the theory names as its parent. Document draws
the ten diagram views and writes the preregistration and the audit dossier.
Simulate propagates the construct network from one value for every construct or
from an impulse in one of them. Literature maps the small demonstration corpus,
the frozen OpenAlex corpus of works on panic disorder or a corpus you upload, and
builds the theory's landscape on it. The articles
'Developing and testing a theory' and 'Mapping the literature' explain what each
function computes.

## The theory editor

The editor shows the theory as forms, one card for each construct, proposition,
phenomenon, prediction, assumption, alternative, evidence entry and test
outcome, beside a source pane that holds the same theory as YAML or JSON. Either
side can be edited. Each change is read by the package's reader, validated in
full and scored with the checklist, so the problems shown beside the fields and
the score above them are the package's own. A change in the forms rewrites the
source in the package's layout, which keeps no comments. New theory starts from
an empty template, and the version fields offer to record the current content
hash.

Import DAGitty takes model code copied from [dagitty.net](https://dagitty.net)
or from the dagitty package and reads it with `tf_read_dagitty()`, as the Get
started vignette describes. Each variable becomes a construct and each edge a
proposition, and the import window shows the R code that makes the same theory. The
imported theory replaces the one in the editor and needs a definition for each
construct before it validates.

## Saving a theory and reproducing a result

Save YAML in the editor writes the theory with the package's writer, so the file
reads back as the same theory, with the same content hash, in R and in Python.
Below each result, the code panel gives the R code that reproduces it with the
installed package, with buttons to copy it or download it as a script. The code
reads an example theory through `tf_example_path()`, and for any other theory it
reads a file that you save beside the script first, under the name the code
gives. To reproduce a result on a theory you edited, save it with Save YAML,
download the script into the same folder and run it there with `theoryforge`
installed.

## Sharing a view

Copy link writes the theory and the chosen operation into the part of the
address after `#`, which browsers do not send to the server. An example travels
as its name and any other theory as its text, compressed. Links are kept below
16,000 characters so that mail and chat programs pass them on whole, and a
larger theory is better sent as a file. A prior version, rival or corpus that
you uploaded is not carried by the link. A link pasted into a tab that already
shows the app opens there, once an operation that is running has finished. The
apps keep the session and the colour theme in the browser's storage where the
browser allows it, and run without it where it does not. The session is the only
copy of edits that Save YAML has not written, so choosing an example, uploading
a file, starting a new theory or opening a link that would replace an edited
theory asks first.

## Limits

The apps fetch no research data over the network. The literature operations read
the corpora listed above, so `tf_fetch_corpus()` is not offered: run it in the
package and upload the file it writes. Three other functions stay in the
installed package. The embedding screen needs an embedding model, and rendering
a report with `tf_render_report()` needs Quarto. The OSF deposit needs a
personal access token, which a web page should not hold. Each engine is a fixed
release, so the package runs under the language version that release provides,
which can differ from yours. The R app also downloads the jsonlite and yaml
packages from the webR package repository when it starts. The repository's
[apps/README.md](https://github.com/pablobernabeu/theoryforge/blob/main/apps/README.md)
gives the engine versions and how the apps are built and tested.
